items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I did so many things with Milt that it’s hard for me to cite any one experience... I could always count on Milt to play anything I wrote and to embellish it

ctx.x: And you had top guys playing on the sessions, right?

Well yeah. Well now you’re getting into the studio scene in New York, which I was lucky enough to get into in the 1950s and stayed with into the 1980s. There were several hundred, as I estimate, it couldn’t have been more than maybe two hundred people who did most of the recording work in New York and by recording I mean not only the commercials for dozens of producers around town, but the phonograph records, which were all ad hoc kind of orchestras — Andre Kostelanetz, Percy Faith, those were typical of the…
So if you were listening to Andrew Kostelanetz, and then you listened to Percy Faith —

items.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: Dick Hyman called me for a Fender record date.

ctx.x: And you showed him, then he turned right around and was able to show you.

He sure did. I took him down in the basement of my house and there we were and we had practice with the radio. And I was, and Dick Hyman called me for a Fender record date. And I said, “Oh my Lord, here I’ve got this Sidewinder.” And everybody else got their regular instrument, and I walked in there with this Fender bass. And we got to playing and I’m playing the thing and I don’t know nothing. I knew the fingering but I don’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
know nothing about equipment. And the engineer said to me he says, “Ja, Ja, will you give me a little more highs?” And I start to go up this way.

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And as much as I love playing with rhythm sections and with great people like Milt

ctx.x: But to do studio work like that it’s obvious that you had to be able to sight read and do things in a short time.

Well see a lot of us began playing jazz and then got into studio work, and were able to use some of that jazz expertise in one way or another in studio work. The improvisation for a pianist always came in very handy. And then the studio work taught us a lot of other things like in my case I began to play organ as well as to read and learn how to arrange © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

and conduct and so forth. And then the funny thing is, and when I use the plural I mean people like not only myself but people like Milt Hinton and Bob Rosengarden and I’m thinking of present company and certain other guys. The funny thing is that after a while the studio work came to an end and we all became entirely jazz people after that, again. So it was a kind of hiatus that might have lasted decades but it was a kind of a wonderful hiatus.

items.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dick Hyman orchestrated me… for the symphony orchestra for eight basses and we did it with a lot of basses.

ctx.x: I was playing up at Wells in Harlem and he come in and we said, “Boy, you don‟t know anything about this”, and he‟d sit down and I said, “You‟re right, I don‟t” [laughter].
Dick Hyman… I spoke to Dick Hyman about it. He gave Dick Hyman his first job in Harlem.

Right, at Wells, yeah, because he used to come in all the time. He loved piano players. He used to tell Joe Wells, he said, “Look, you‟ve got to have a piano player I can come listen to” [laugher]. He said, “I don‟t want to hear this” [laughter].
